beats.say: A to the power X plus one, over B to the power Y minus two, all squared,
times B to the power X plus two, over A to the power three minus Y, equals A to the power nine B.
asks: Which part is the second fraction?

beats.say: Find X and Y. Two unknowns need two equations: the bases A and B give one each.
asks: How can one equation give two answers?

beats.say: The plan: tidy each side into one power of A times one power of B.
asks: What does one power of A mean?

beats.say: Then the powers of A must match, and the powers of B must match.
Step one, do the power first: the bracket must go before we can group the bases.
Squaring a fraction squares its top and its bottom.
asks: Does the square go to the top and bottom?

beats.say: Now times power: a power of a power, multiply the powers.
So A to the power two times X plus one, over B to the power two times Y minus two.
Expand the brackets: two X plus two on top, two Y minus four below. Then put it back into the equation.
Step two, group the same bases. Multiplying fractions: tops together, bottoms together.
asks: Why can I join the two fractions?

beats.say: Step three, divide. The same base is on top and bottom, so minus the powers: top power minus bottom power.
Keep the brackets: the whole bottom power is taken away.
asks: Why do I need the brackets?

beats.say: Step four, tidy each power. For A: two X plus two, minus the bracket three minus Y.
asks: Why tidy one power at a time?

beats.say: Minus a bracket flips every sign inside: the three becomes minus three, and minus Y becomes plus Y.
asks: Why does minus Y become plus Y?

do.text: Minus a bracket flips every sign inside

beats.say: Collect the terms: two X plus Y minus one.
asks: How do I collect the terms?

beats.say: For B: X plus two, minus the bracket two Y minus four.
asks: Which is the bottom power for b?

beats.say: Again every sign flips: minus two Y, and plus four.
asks: Why does minus four become plus four?

beats.say: Collect the terms: X minus two Y plus six.
asks: Where does the six come from?

beats.say: So the left side is A to the power two X plus Y minus one,
asks: Where does this power come from?

beats.say: times B to the power X minus two Y plus six.
asks: Is the left side tidy now?

beats.say: On the right, a bare B means B to the power one, so write it in.
asks: Why is b the same as b to the power 1?

beats.say: Step five, compare the powers of each base. First the base A.

read: The equation is true for every value of $a$ and $b$.
Take $b = 1$: every power of $b$ is $1$, so only the $a$ parts are left.
Two powers of the same base are equal only when the powers are equal.
**Same base on both sides: the powers must match.**

beats.say: Same base A on both sides, so the powers are equal: two X plus Y minus one equals nine.
Now the base B: its powers are equal too.
asks: Why are the b powers equal?

beats.say: X minus two Y plus six equals one, the one from the bare B.
Step six, solve together. Add one to the A equation: two X plus Y equals ten.
asks: How do I solve two equations together?

beats.say: Make Y the subject, so it can go into the B equation: Y equals ten minus two X.
Substitute: X minus two times, ten minus two X, plus six equals one.
Expand: X minus twenty plus four X plus six equals one.
Collect: five X equals fifteen, so X equals three.
Then Y equals ten minus two times three: four.
So X equals three and Y equals four.
